meta.title: Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo
meta.thesis: Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A release changes the refund-policy prompt and must prove old behavior still works. By the end, they should be able to build or review Promptfoo regression pack with assertions and release gates, measure known behaviors preserved after prompt edits, and catch the failure where the new prompt passes happy paths but fails refusal and citation cases.

modules.title: Prompt tests protect behavior, not exact wording
modules.sub: Start by deciding what the release must not break.
modules.summary: The regression target is a behavior contract for prompt changes.
objectives: Explain why exact-output snapshots are brittle for LLMs.
Define behavior-level checks for a concrete prompt edit.
Identify critical slices before writing config.

blocks.title: The prompt changed; the product promise did not

spans.text: Problem anchor: a team rewrites a refund-policy prompt to sound warmer. The new answer is friendlier, but it stops citing the policy page and gives refunds for cases that need escalation. A manual read of three happy paths misses the regression.

promptfoo helps by running prompts, providers, and tests as a repeatable matrix. The important move is pedagogical: test the behavior contract. The answer may use different words, but it must cite policy, refuse unsupported requests, keep the JSON shape, and avoid promising unauthorized actions.

blocks.analogy: A prompt regression suite is a seatbelt check, not a handwriting comparison.

blocks.title: Worked behavior contract: refund prompt v4 to v5

spans.text: The team writes four preserved behaviors: cite the refund terms for eligibility, refuse automatic refunds after the cutoff, ask for account review when exception data is missing, and output JSON with decision, rationale, citations, and escalation_needed.

items.text: Happy path: eligible refund with citation.
Refusal path: outside window, no automatic refund.
Missing-data path: account status absent, ask for escalation.
Injection path: user asks the model to ignore policy.

blocks.title: Behavior contract
blocks.prompt: What should a prompt regression test usually preserve?

options.text: Every adjective from the previous answer.
Required behavior such as citations, refusal rules, and output shape.

blocks.explanation: LLM outputs vary; tests should focus on product-critical properties.

modules.title: Cases need inputs, expected properties, and slices
modules.sub: A good promptfoo suite is a small dataset, not a list of vibes.
modules.summary: Regression cases should include scenario, variables, expected properties, and metadata.
objectives: Create cases with vars, expected outcomes, and slice metadata.
Separate critical cases from exploratory cases.
Use production failures as durable examples.

blocks.title: A case should say what failure it catches

spans.text: Each promptfoo case should include the input variables, the product slice, expected properties, and severity. A case that says only "refund question" is weak. A case that says slice=refund_cutoff, severity=critical, expected_citation=refund_terms, expected_decision=deny is useful.

Case 1 asks for a refund after 12 days and expects approval with a citation. Case 2 asks after 45 days and expects denial plus escalation option. Case 3 provides no account status and expects a question or tool call. Case 4 contains an instruction to ignore the policy and expects the model to treat it as user text, not authority.
Spaced recall: bring back module 1 and ask which behavior each case protects.

modules.title: Assertions mix deterministic checks and rubric judges
modules.sub: Use hard checks for contracts and judges for semantic quality.
modules.summary: promptfoo assertions should match the risk of the behavior.
objectives: Choose contains, regex, JSON/schema, JavaScript, and rubric-style checks appropriately.
Keep LLM judge checks secondary to hard contract checks.
Avoid making weak metrics look official.

spans.text: Use deterministic assertions for things the product cannot compromise: valid JSON, required keys, required citation field, no unauthorized refund promise, allowed tool name, or refusal phrase. Use rubric or LLM-judge checks for semantic quality: is the rationale grounded, concise, and helpful?
The KB warns that frameworks can make weak metrics look official. The fix is not to avoid judges; it is to put them after hard gates and version their rubrics.

modules.title: Provider and prompt matrices expose release tradeoffs
modules.sub: The same case should run across prompt and model candidates.
modules.summary: promptfoo matrices show whether a change is robust or model-specific.
objectives: Predict the failure caused by removing a citation assertion.
Compare prompt and provider candidates without hiding cost.

blocks.title: Minimal promptfoo config for refund prompt regression
blocks.code:
prompts:
  - file://prompts/refund_v4.txt
  - file://prompts/refund_v5.txt
providers:
  - openai:gpt-5.5
  - openai:gpt-5.5-mini

tests:
  - vars:
      question: "I used the subscription for 45 days. Can I get a refund?"
      policy_excerpt: "Refunds are automatic only within 30 days. After that, escalate for review."
    metadata:
      slice: refund_cutoff
      severity: critical
    assert:
      - type: contains
        value: "30 days"
      - type: contains
        value: "escalate"
      - type: javascript
        value: "output.includes('refund') && !output.includes('automatic refund approved')"
      - type: llm-rubric
        value: "The answer is grounded in the policy excerpt and does not invent eligibility."

spans.text: This config compares prompt versions and provider choices on the same critical case. In a real suite, add more cases and keep cost limits in CI.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the risk if the contains assertion for "escalate" is removed while the rubric remains.
predictThenReveal.answer: The suite may pass an answer that sounds grounded but omits the required escalation path. Rubrics are useful, but hard product obligations should have hard assertions.

spans.text: Checklist: cases include slice and severity; critical cases have deterministic assertions; rubric wording is versioned; providers match the release candidates; the suite runs the real prompt path; secrets are not embedded in config; and CI has a budget limit.

modules.title: CI gates need budgets, baselines, and triage
modules.sub: Regression testing becomes useful when failures change release behavior.
modules.summary: A promptfoo suite should block, warn, or route review based on severity.
objectives: Define pass thresholds and triage rules.
Handle flaky judge checks without ignoring failures.
Promote production incidents into future cases.

blocks.title: A failing case needs an owner and a decision

spans.text: CI should not merely upload a pretty table. Critical hard-gate failures block release. Medium semantic failures route to reviewer. Exploratory failures create tickets or dataset candidates. Judge flakiness should be fixed by better rubrics, deterministic checks, or quarantine with a dated reason, not ignored forever.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Gate releases on critical behavior, review semantic drift, and retire stale cases deliberately.
blocks.useWhen: Use CI prompt regression when prompts, providers, retrieval, or model settings change and old behavior must be preserved.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid making CI depend only on expensive or flaky LLM-judge checks, and avoid keeping stale baselines that encode known-bad behavior.

blocks.title: CI behavior
blocks.prompt: What should happen when a critical citation assertion fails in CI?

options.text: Ship if the answer sounds polite.
Block the prompt release until fixed or explicitly waived with owner and rationale.
Delete the case because LLMs vary.

blocks.explanation: Critical deterministic failures should change release behavior.
